title: Which AI to use for each thing
promise: By the end you'll be able to decide in under a minute which of the four AIs to use for each task in your project. And you'll know how much you're going to pay a month for it.
why: Javier sells specialty coffee in Gijón and wanted to set up his online store. He subscribed to ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Google AI Pro all on the same day, just in case. That was $66 a month for five months: $330 to use all three for exactly the same thing. By the time the one task only one of them handled well finally showed up, he'd already burned through the store's budget. Choosing well isn't about finding the best AI on the planet. It's about not paying three times for the same thing. And knowing which one to turn to when the other gets stuck.

theory.title: The four do almost the same thing, and that's the trap
theory.text: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot share 80% of whatever you're going to think of asking them. Drafting an awkward email. Explaining what a database is. Writing the code for a page with a contact form. All four do those things, and do them well. If you test a simple task on all four, the answers will look so similar you'll think it doesn't matter which one you use. The difference lives in the remaining 20%. That 20% shows up exactly when your project starts getting real: with a long file, with two hours of conversation piled up, or when you need it to remember what you decided yesterday. The doubt creeping in now is: if I choose wrong, do I mess things up? No. Switching from one to another costs zero dollars: there's no lock-in, nothing to migrate, and your old conversations stay right where they were. The expensive part isn't choosing wrong. The expensive part is paying for three subscriptions at once without being able to say what each one is for.
theory.analogy: It's like choosing between four cars that all get you to the supermarket. The difference only shows up the day you climb a mountain pass with a full trunk.
theory.example: Same assignment to all three: write the homepage copy for a coffee shop. All three came back with something publishable in under twenty seconds and it was hard to pick. Second assignment: read these 180 customer emails and pull out the ten most common complaints. There, only two handled the whole file without trimming it along the way.

theory.title: The scorecard: where each one wins
theory.text: ChatGPT is the most generalist and the one that'll surprise you least. It wins at generating images and at talking by voice from your phone. It also wins at searching the internet and summarizing what it finds. And it has a huge catalog of assistants other people have already built. Claude wins at writing. It produces long text that doesn't sound robotic and, above all, long code that works on the first try more often. It also shows you the finished website in a panel next to the chat. That way you see what you're building without installing a single thing. Gemini wins on size and on Google. It swallows giant documents and whole YouTube videos. It lives inside Gmail, Docs, and Drive. And its free plan is the most generous of the four. Copilot plays a different game. It's not a chat you tell your idea to. It's a helper that lives inside the code editor, the program where a website's files get opened and saved. It fills in the lines as you type them. If you've never coded, Copilot is the last one you need, not the first: it completes the code of someone who already knows what they want to write. The short rule so you don't have to think about it every time. Idea, text, or image: ChatGPT. Building something that works: Claude. Huge documents or things that already live in Google: Gemini. A project with twenty files open in an editor: Copilot. And one more thing nobody tells you. Whichever one you use daily will end up being the one you understand best, not the one that wins the rankings.
theory.example: Marta manages a dental clinic in Seville and had three tasks. Turning 200 scanned patient records into a spreadsheet: Gemini, because of the file size. Writing the clinic's website: Claude, because she sees it working as it's written. Preparing Instagram posts with her photo: ChatGPT, for the images. Total paid: one $20 subscription and two free accounts.

theory.title: What it really costs: $0, $20, and the jump to $200
theory.text: All four have a free plan, and the free one covers far more than people think. The normal paid plan runs around $20 a month across the three chats. ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Google AI Pro sit in that range. Copilot Pro is the cheap one: about $10 a month. What you buy with that $20 isn't more intelligence: it's more quantity. More messages before it cuts you off. More uploaded files and more continuous working time. And access to the models that pause to reason instead of answering fast. Above that there's a step that's scary. ChatGPT Pro and Claude Max run around $200 a month, and Google AI Ultra goes past $270. That tier is built for someone who uses AI six hours a day and hits the ceiling every afternoon. If you're starting out, you'll notice very little difference and you'll have spent ten times more. Money warning: subscriptions renew automatically every month. The current month's charge normally isn't refundable. So if you try an expensive plan, turn off auto-renew the same day you sign up. You'll keep it until the paid month runs out. These prices are for reference and change every few months. Task 3 in this lesson teaches you to check them yourself in two minutes. That's the only figure you can trust.
theory.example: Ana, a freelancer in Bilbao, paid for the $229 plan for a whole month to write her website. She counted her messages afterward: 40 a day. The $22 plan would have been plenty. She burned $207 by not measuring her usage for two days before signing up.

theory.title: The context window: why it forgets your project halfway through
theory.text: The limit that's really going to hurt you isn't the price: it's working memory. In the jargon it's called the context window, meaning everything the AI can have in front of it at once. Your messages, its answers, and the files you upload all take up room in that window. When it fills up, it doesn't warn you with an alarm: it starts forgetting the beginning. It changes your store's name, rewrites a part you'd already fixed an hour ago, contradicts a decision you made together. Sizes vary a lot between them. Gemini is by far the biggest: on the order of 750,000 words, about seven books. Claude runs around 150,000 words, one long book. ChatGPT depends a lot on which plan you have. When you notice it losing the plot, don't argue with it or scold it. Open a new chat and paste in a summary of where you are. You ask it for that summary itself before closing the old chat. It's the trick that'll save you the most headaches in the whole course. The exact numbers change every few months, but the symptom never changes. If it starts repeating itself or contradicting itself, the window is full.
theory.analogy: It's a work desk, not a filing cabinet. It sees everything that fits on top; whatever falls to the floor stops existing for it. Gemini has a twelve-seat dining table; ChatGPT on the free plan has a camping table.

theory.title: The rule of one paid and two free
theory.text: Pick one paid one, whichever you use for the task you repeat most, and keep the other two open free in another tab. If your project is building something (a website, a store, an assistant for your work), pay for Claude. If it's writing, researching, making images, and tinkering with a bit of everything, pay for ChatGPT. If you live inside Gmail and Drive and handle heavy documents, pay for Google AI Pro. The other two, on free, cover two specific gaps. One: getting a second opinion when the paid one insists on a mistake it won't fix. Two: absorbing the big tasks your subscription chokes on. Changing your mind the following month is normal, not a failure: you cancel, stop paying, sign up for the other one. And the most useful warning in this lesson. Don't pay for the second subscription yet. Wait until you can say out loud what specific task the first one doesn't solve for you. If that sentence doesn't come out, you don't need the second one.
theory.example: Javier, the Gijón coffee guy, stuck with just Claude Pro, $22 a month, for the store. When he needed to dig through his supplier's catalog, a 340-page PDF, he uploaded it to free Gemini, asked for the summary, and pasted it into Claude. Extra cost of that move: $0.

theory.title: The five mistakes that'll cost you money or headaches
theory.text: One: paying for several at once on day one. That's what Javier did, and it's $330 that never came back. Two: signing up for the $200 plan just to be safe. What you're usually missing isn't power: it's knowing how to ask for things. That jump multiplies the bill by ten and the result by very little. Three: installing Copilot without being able to read code. It'll keep suggesting lines nonstop and you won't be able to tell the good one from the one that breaks your website. Four, and this one's serious: free and personal plans can use your conversations to train, unless you turn that off in Settings. So don't paste a client list, a payroll sheet, an ID, or a medical report into a free chat without checking that box first. It's not paranoia: it's a data protection law issue. Five: trusting a comparison video from a year ago, because it describes a world that no longer exists. And an extra one almost nobody sees coming: don't ask an AI which AI is best. It has no access to the others and hasn't tried them. What it knows about them, it read in old text. And it'll still answer with total confidence while guessing.

tasks.title: Open the three free accounts in one sitting
tasks.action: Go to chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and gemini.google.com. On all three, click the button top right. Depending on the page it says Sign up or Log in. Sign in with your Google account: it's the fastest and saves you inventing another password. None of them will ask for a card for the free plan. If a screen asking for a card number shows up, you clicked the upgrade plan button. Go back with the browser arrow. Leave all three tabs open, you'll use them in the next tasks. We'll leave Copilot for later: it needs a code editor installed and right now it gets you nothing.
tasks.expect: Three tabs with an empty text box waiting for you to type, and your name or initial top right on all three.
tasks.stuck: If Gemini tells you it's not available, check that you signed in with a personal Gmail account and not a work one. Company admins often have it blocked. If Claude asks for a phone number to verify, that's normal and it's only used once.

tasks.title: Send the same assignment to all three and compare with your own eyes
tasks.where: In the three tabs you just opened
tasks.action: Copy the prompt below, meaning the assignment you write for it. Paste it exactly into ChatGPT, then Claude, then Gemini. Don't change a single comma between one and the next: change the assignment and the comparison is worthless. Once you have all three answers, read them in a row. Write down on paper which one you liked best, and above all why. Five minutes total.
tasks.prompt:
You're a copywriter and web developer. I want the homepage for an online specialty coffee shop called Northern Roast, in Gijón, Spain. It sells three coffees: Ethiopia ($13.90), Colombia ($12.50), and house blend ($10.90). The audience is people 30 to 50 who already buy whole bean coffee and want something better than the supermarket kind.

Give me three things, in this order, each with its own heading:

1. The page's copy: headline, subheadline, three sales blocks, and a final call to action. Warm tone, plain English, no brochure words like excellence, passion, or unique experience.

2. The complete HTML and CSS code for that page in a single file, looking good on mobile, with no external libraries or internet links.

3. The three things you think will go wrong once this store has real customers, and what you'd do about each one.

If you're missing any piece of data to do this well, tell me at the end instead of making it up.
tasks.expect: Three answers with the same three-section structure. You'll see clear differences: one gives you the most complete code, another the most natural text, another warns you about more issues. That comparison, done with your own real assignment, is worth more than any ranking you read out there.
tasks.stuck: If one gets stuck mid-code, just write continue and it'll pick up exactly where it left off. If one refuses, saying it can't write code, redo the prompt in a new chat. Sometimes it drags confusion along from an earlier conversation.

tasks.title: Check today's prices with your own eyes
tasks.action: Open these four pages: openai.com/chatgpt/pricing, claude.com/pricing, one.google.com/about/ai-plans, and github.com/features/copilot/plans. Look for the dollar price, not any other currency that shows up by default. Write down all four numbers in a note on your phone with today's date next to them. Also check each free plan's fine print. See how many messages a day it gives you and whether it lets you upload files. Also check whether you can use the good model or only the fast one.
tasks.expect: Four prices written down with a date. If any is way off from the figures in this lesson, the official page's number is the right one. Prices change every few months and this lesson doesn't.
tasks.stuck: If the page insists on showing a different currency, scroll to the footer and change the country to the US. Another option: go into the payment screen without actually paying, since the final amount shows up there. If you can't find the free plan in the table, it's usually the leftmost column, the one without a colored button.

tasks.title: Ask the AI to choose for you, with your case on the table
tasks.where: In the Claude tab, or whichever you liked best in task 2
tasks.action: Paste the prompt below and fill in the brackets with your real situation before sending it. Be honest about the budget: if you write that you have $200 a month, it's going to recommend $200-a-month things. Once it answers, save that response in a document. It's your decision criteria for the next few months.
tasks.prompt:
Act as an independent advisor, not a salesperson. I'm going to describe my situation and I want you to decide for me which AI subscription to pay for and which ones to use free.

My situation:
- What I want to build: [describe your idea in two sentences]
- My coding experience: none, and the terminal intimidates me.
- Hours I'll dedicate a week: [X]
- Maximum monthly budget: $[X].
- Tools I already use daily: [Gmail, Excel, Notion, whatever]

Give me the answer like this:
1. One single recommended subscription, with its price and the specific reason in one sentence.
2. Which two I'd use free and for exactly what task each one.
3. The specific signal that'll tell me I need to upgrade, something measurable like: when it cuts you off three days in a row before six in the evening.
4. What I should NOT pay for yet, and why.

Let me know if any price you mention might be outdated and tell me which page to check it on.
tasks.expect: A recommendation of ONE single subscription, with a price, and a list of what you don't need yet. If it recommends paying for two or three, reply reminding it of your budget and ask it to pick one.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you a generic speech about the advantages of each one, reply with this: I don't want an analysis, I want a decision. One single subscription, and why that one and not the others.

tasks.title: Measure where the free plan cuts you off
tasks.where: In whichever free AI you've used most this week
tasks.action: Work a normal day with it without holding back and write down two things. One: what time the "limit reached" warning shows up. Two: what it offers instead, meaning waiting a few hours, switching to a faster and worse model, or paying. Repeat it a second day. With two days you have the only data point you need. It'll tell you whether that $20 a month buys you something real or is a whim.
tasks.expect: A message like you've reached your limit, come back at 6:40 PM. Or an automatic switch to a simpler model, without much warning. If you haven't seen it in two days, your usage fits comfortably in free and you don't need to pay anything yet.
tasks.stuck: If it cuts you off after ten minutes, that doesn't mean you use it a lot. It means you're uploading large files or asking for images, and that eats up far more than writing. Try a day with just text to get a clean reading.

tasks.title: Put its memory to the test with a big document
tasks.where: In Gemini and Claude, with the same file
tasks.action: Find the longest PDF you have handy: a contract, an instruction manual, a supplier's catalog, a syllabus. Upload it with the paperclip button right next to the text box. Do it in both and paste the same prompt into both. What you're measuring isn't who summarizes better, it's which one tells you the truth about what it managed to read.
tasks.prompt:
I've uploaded a document for you. Before summarizing it, tell me how many pages you actually managed to read and whether you had to leave any out.

Then:
1. Summarize the document in ten points, ordered from most to least important.
2. Quote me the exact page each point comes from.
3. Tell me three things the document assumes but never actually explains.
4. If you left any part unread, tell me clearly in the FIRST line of your answer. I'd rather hear you couldn't than get an incomplete summary that looks complete.
tasks.expect: A summary with page numbers next to each point. The real test is in the first line. One will admit it read 40 of 340 pages. That one is being far more useful to you than the one pretending it read the whole thing.
tasks.stuck: The PDF might be a scan, meaning photos of pages instead of text you can select with your mouse. In that case it might read nothing. Upload a single page as an image and ask what it says: that way you'll know whether the problem is size or file format.

tasks.title: Create a Project with fixed instructions and stop repeating yourself
tasks.where: In Claude's left sidebar, or ChatGPT's
tasks.action: In Claude, click Projects in the left column and then Create project. Name it after your idea. In ChatGPT it's called Projects and is in the same spot, with almost the same button. Inside you'll see a box for the project's instructions. Paste the text below into it, changing the part about your idea. From then on, every chat you open inside that project already knows who you are and what you're doing. You save yourself explaining it twenty times.
tasks.prompt:
FIXED CONTEXT FOR THIS PROJECT

Who I am: I don't know how to code. I've never used a terminal and it intimidates me. I work on Windows.

What I'm building: [your idea in two sentences].

How I want you to talk to me:
- Plain English, short sentences.
- Every technical word, translated in parentheses the first time.
- Never assume I know where a button is: tell me its exact name and where on the screen it is.

How I want the code:
- Complete files, never loose fragments like here's your previous code.
- Always tell me the file's name and which folder it goes in.
- If something needs to run in the terminal, warn me first and explain what that command does.

Limits:
- If something costs money, tell me how much in dollars before recommending it.
- If an action is irreversible (deleting, publishing, paying), warn me IN CAPITAL LETTERS before doing it.
- If you're not sure about something, say so. I'd rather have an I don't know than a made-up fact.
tasks.expect: The project shows up with its name in the left column and the instructions saved. Open a new chat inside it and just type hello: it should reply already knowing what you're building, without you telling it.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see Projects, your plan might not include it yet. In the meantime, save that text in a phone note and paste it at the start of every new chat. It works exactly the same, just with copy and paste.

tasks.title: Get a second opinion when one gets stuck
tasks.where: In an AI different from the one that got stuck
tasks.action: Once you've had three attempts at the same error and the AI keeps insisting on the same fix that doesn't work, stop. Open a different one of the three. Instead of telling it the whole story, paste the prompt below with the error message exactly as it appeared, not summarized or translated. The second one not having seen what the first one did is exactly what sometimes gets it right on the first try.
tasks.prompt:
Another assistant has had three tries and hasn't fixed this, and I want a fresh opinion. Don't assume what it did was right.

What I'm trying to achieve: [one sentence].
What I did: [paste the steps you followed].
The exact error I'm getting, copied without changing anything:
[paste the whole error, every line]
What I've already tried that didn't work: [list].

Give me:
1. What you think is really happening, in one sentence, no jargon.
2. The fastest check to confirm you're right, before touching anything.
3. The fix, with the complete file if code needs to change.
4. If you think the problem isn't what I think it is, tell me straight even if it annoys me.
tasks.expect: A different diagnosis from the first AI's. If both agree on the cause, that's the cause, and the failure is in how the fix is being applied. If they disagree, you now have two paths to try instead of one.
tasks.stuck: If the second one also gets stuck, the problem is almost never the AI: it's a piece of data you're taking for granted that it's missing. Describe the problem again as if telling it to someone who just walked in the door and has seen nothing.

tasks.title: Turn off auto-renewal the same day you sign up
tasks.where: In the subscription settings, inside the app you paid for
tasks.action: The day you pay for your first subscription, go straight into your name, top right. Look for Settings and, inside, Billing or Subscription. Turn off auto-renewal there. WARNING: this doesn't take anything away from you. You keep the paid plan through the last day of the month you bought. All you're avoiding is being charged for another month without noticing. If you want to keep using it the following month, you turn it back on in two clicks. Companies don't usually refund a month already started. So this one minute saves you $20 every time you'd forget.
tasks.expect: A message like your plan will stay active until September 18, and the renewal toggle off or grayed out. Write that date in your phone's calendar two days ahead.
tasks.stuck: If you paid from the mobile app, the cancellation isn't on the AI's website. It's in the App Store or Google Play, under Subscriptions. That's the exact spot where most people leave a charge running for months.

matters: The price isn't the limit that's going to hurt. Two others hurt: the daily message cap and the memory that fills up mid-afternoon. Choose by looking only at the dollar-per-month and you'll end up with an expensive plan that still doesn't fix the bottleneck.
Switching AI mid-project is free, fast, and normal. Someone who spends three days fighting the same one is confusing two things: giving up on that tool and giving up on their project.

What you write in a chat can end up training the model if you don't turn that off in Settings. Pasting a client list, a payroll sheet, or a medical report into a free chat isn't paranoid caution. It's a legal problem with fines attached.

Comparisons expire within months. A video from a year ago saying which one's best describes a world that no longer exists. That's why this lesson teaches you to measure it yourself in two minutes, instead of handing you a ranking that rots.
ignore: Model names and version numbers. They change every few months. In the app it's enough to leave whatever comes selected by default: it's almost always right for what you're doing.
Scoreboards where one gets 92.1 and another 91.7. You'll never notice that difference in your coffee shop. What you will notice is which one cuts you off at six in the evening.

The API, which is the side door for connecting AI to a program of yours, paying by usage. It exists, it's powerful, and it's cheap at volume. But it's handled with code, and right now it solves nothing the app doesn't already solve for you.
canDo: Compare itself against the others on checkable things: what file size it accepts, whether it reads scanned PDFs, whether it generates images, whether it searches the internet.
Warn you a task is too big for it, as long as you ask it clearly in the prompt. If you don't ask, it tends to pretend it handled all of it.
Translate your vague idea into a list of specific tasks and point out which one actually decides which tool suits you.
Summarize its own conversation so you can paste it into another AI when switching. Just ask: summarize this chat so another assistant can pick up from here.
cantDo: Know its own price today. Plans change after it's trained, so it'll give you old figures with total confidence. Always check the official page.
Objectively tell you which one's best. None of them has tried the others, they don't have access to each other, and each one roots for its own team.
See what happened in your chat with another AI. It can't even see one of its own other chats, unless you paste it in yourself or it's inside the same Project.
Cancel a subscription, change your plan, or ask for a refund for you. You do that yourself on the company's website: no AI touches your wallet for you.
words: The brain that actually thinks up the answer. ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini are the apps you type into. Inside each one there's one or several models, and sometimes you can pick which to use from a dropdown.
Everything the AI can have in front of it at once: your messages, its answers, and the files you upload. When it fills up, it starts forgetting the first things you told it.
The tiny piece the AI splits text into so it can count it. Roughly three-quarters of a word in English, so a thousand tokens is about 750 words.
The assignment you type into the text box. The better you tell it what you want, for whom, and with what limits, the better what it gives back.
When it makes up a fact and tells you with the same confidence as a true one. Prices, dates, laws, and web addresses are where it happens most.
That besides reading text it understands photos, audio, or video. Taking a photo of an invoice and having it pull out the amounts is multimodal.
The program where a website's or app's files get opened and saved. It's similar to a word processor, but for program files. The most used one is called VS Code.
The side door through which another program talks to the AI without a person typing. It's paid by amount used instead of a flat monthly fee.
The cap on messages or files your plan allows within a stretch of time. Hit it and it makes you wait a few hours or drops you to a faster, less capable version.
